California probate · a plain guide

What happens now

If you have been named to handle someone's estate, you have been given a job you did not apply for, at a time you would not have chosen. This is what the process looks like, roughly how long each part takes, and — the part nobody explains — which professional answers which question, so you stop paying for the wrong advice.

Nothing here is legal or tax advice, and it is not specific to your estate. It is a map, so that when you talk to your attorney you already know what you are looking at. Every rule below has exceptions, and yours may be one of them.

The sequence, and roughly how long

1
Where it starts

A petition is filed with the county Superior Court asking it to open probate and appoint someone to act — the executor if there is a will, an administrator if there is not. You do not have authority yet. This is the hardest part to sit through, because the responsibility arrives before the ability to do anything.

2
About four to eight weeks

Notice is published in a local paper and mailed to everyone entitled to it, and the court sets a hearing. Nothing much is required of you here except to wait, and to keep the house insured and the bills paid.

3
The hearing — the day it changes

The court appoints you and issues Letters. This single page is the document that proves you can act. Banks, title companies and insurers will all ask for it. Keep several certified copies. It also states how much authority you were given, which decides almost everything about selling a property.

4
Within about four months

A probate referee — appointed by the court, not chosen by you — appraises the property and other non-cash assets. Their figure becomes the estate's official value. If a sale has to be confirmed by the court, that figure is the number it is measured against.

5
Four months, running alongside

Creditors have a window to make claims. This is a large part of why an estate cannot simply be wound up quickly, even when everyone agrees.

6
Any time after step 3

If the property is to be sold, it can be sold. How depends on your authority: either like an ordinary sale with written notice to the heirs beforehand, or through a court hearing where other buyers are allowed to bid against the accepted offer. Your attorney will tell you which applies to you.

7
Nine to eighteen months, commonly

A final accounting, distribution to the beneficiaries, and discharge. Estates with a property to sell, a dispute, or a tax filing take longer. Very few take less.

Who answers which question

Most of the frustration in probate comes from asking the right question of the wrong person. This is the division.

Your probate attorney

Authority, deadlines, court filings, creditor claims, disagreements among heirs, whether you can rent the property out, what your own liability looks like.

Ask first: “What authority do my Letters give me, and can I sell without a court hearing?” Everything else about the property follows from that.

A CPA or tax adviser

The estate's tax filings, the cost basis of the property, capital gains if it is sold, and whether keeping the house triggers a property-tax reassessment under Proposition 19.

Ask early, not at the end: “If we keep the house rather than sell it, what happens to the property taxes?” In this county that answer is often large enough to change the decision, and it is far easier to plan for than to undo.

The probate referee

The court's own appraisal of the property. You do not choose them and you do not negotiate with them. Their value is a formal step, not an opinion of what a buyer would pay today.

A real estate broker — what I actually do

What the property is worth, what it would take to sell it, and how to get it emptied, cleared and presented. I can put a written opinion of value in your hands, dated to the date of death, which your attorney and your CPA will both ask for.

What I will not do is tell you whether to sell, answer a tax question, or give you a number over the phone before I have done the work. If I do any of those, get a second opinion about me.

What you can do while you wait

The gap between filing and appointment is the part that feels useless. It is not — these are the things that cause trouble later if they are left.

  • Tell the insurer the house is empty. Most policies limit or drop cover on a vacant property, often after 30 or 60 days, and a claim then fails. A vacancy endorsement is usually straightforward. This is the single most common expensive oversight.
  • Keep the mortgage and property taxes current. They do not pause. If there is a reverse mortgage, tell your attorney this week — those have a short clock after a death.
  • Do not throw anything away yet. Not paperwork, not what looks like junk. Beneficiaries and the court may both need to see it, and things that look worthless sometimes are not.
  • Find the deed, or ask the title company to. How the property was held changes what has to happen, and it is better known early.
  • Write down what you spend. You are generally entitled to be reimbursed for what you lay out, but only if you can show it.
  • Ask whether full probate is even required. California has simpler routes for smaller estates and for property passing between spouses. The thresholds change, so this is a question for your attorney rather than something to read off a website.

Questions people ask, that have short answers

Do I have to clean the house out before it can be sold?

No. It can be sold as it stands, and often that is the better decision. There are companies that clear a house entirely, and the family takes what it wants first.

Can I sell it before probate is finished?

Usually yes — once you have been appointed. The sale does not have to wait for the estate to close.

Do I need a lawyer to do this?

Not legally. California lets you file and act on your own, and people do. But where estates go wrong is almost always the sale, a creditor claim, or a disagreement between heirs — and by then it is more expensive to fix than it would have been to avoid.

My brother and I do not agree about selling.

The person the court appointed has the authority, but a beneficiary who objects can require a hearing. This is a question for the attorney, early, before positions harden.

What is the house worth?

That is a real question with a real answer, and it deserves the work rather than a guess. I will prepare a written opinion of value with the comparable sales behind it, dated to the date of death, at no charge and with no obligation. Most attorneys prefer to have it in the file early.

Am I personally on the hook if I get something wrong?

A personal representative does carry real responsibility. That is exactly why the boring steps — insurance, records, receipts — matter more than they look. Ask your attorney to spell out your duties in writing.

If you want the valuation

It is a written broker's opinion of value: the estate's property, the comparable sales it rests on, a range with a midpoint as of the date of death, and a present-day range alongside it. It is not an appraisal, and it is not the probate referee's valuation — the court arranges that separately, and it is the figure the estate is formally measured against. It is a document to help you and your advisers see the position clearly.

There is no charge and no obligation, and I will send a copy directly to your attorney if you would like. If you never list the property with me, the document is still yours.
